# The Heat Is Urban: How Cities Can Tame Summer's Worst

Summer heat has always been dangerous, but climate change has transformed it from a seasonal inconvenience into a genuine public health crisis. Cities bear the brunt of this transformation—and, in many cases, helped create it. The urban heat island effect, whereby cities run several degrees hotter than surrounding countryside, is not an accident of geography. It is the product of design choices: acres of asphalt, dark rooftops, sparse tree canopy, and building forms that trap heat. The encouraging corollary is that what was designed can be redesigned. Cities possess an arsenal of tools—trees, street design, housing policy, and public transit among them—that can make summer measurably more bearable. The challenge is that these tools come with tradeoffs, and cities must confront them honestly rather than pretending that cooling is free.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

Trees are the most intuitively appealing solution, and among the most effective. A mature shade tree can lower surface temperatures beneath its canopy by 20 to 45 degrees Fahrenheit compared to unshaded pavement, through a combination of shading and evapotranspiration.
